body.text: Toshie Aso was a primary school student when she saw the glowing object in the sky.
Decades later, she has remained emphatic about what it was.
"I have seen a UFO," she said.
In many settings, this would be an eyebrow-raising comment, but not in Iino.

The small town is home to Japan's UFO Museum, an octagonal-shaped building nestled partway up Mount Senganmori, a pyramid-shaped hill that has been linked to UFO sightings for decades — and which has earned Iino the title of "UFO Village" or "Home of Aliens".
It's a moniker the small town has embraced.
Like much of rural Japan, Iino has been struggling with a falling and aging population. It's lost almost half of its residents over the past seven decades.
Locals have turned to the extraterrestrial in a bid to revitalise the town, including hosting an annual festival that attracts thousands of people, many dressed as aliens.

Festival organisers said there had been increasing interest since US President Donald Trump began declassifying and releasing documents on UFOs, now referred to as UAPs (Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena).

In the capital, Tokyo, a Japanese parliamentary group has been considering sightings listed in Pentagon files as being in or near Japan, something politicians argued had serious national security implications.
The 'aliens' descend
You don't have to look far to find an alien in Iino, even on a quiet day.

The road into town offers up the first grey, oval-eyed face: a stone sculpture sitting near a traffic light. On the opposite side of the intersection, a shrub has been pruned to resemble a flying saucer.
On festival day, things are dialled up.
A spacecraft-shaped jumping castle, UFO banners and food stalls offering alien-themed produce adorn the main street.
Then there's the human aliens.
A group of costume-clad young women who "absolutely love aliens" said they had travelled from Tokyo to take part in the festival.
"I think of it as UFO town, I really do," one said.
"Apparently, a UFO even appeared just this week."
Ryuichi Aso, the head of a local development group that runs the festival, said there was a romance and fascination to space.
It was about 50 years ago that the town first started using its extraterrestrial reputation in a revitalisation bid.
Back then the town had about 8,000 people, but its population had already started to decline.
"The town has consistently focused its development specifically on this theme," Aso explained.
The current festival was added about five years ago to "create even more excitement".
The mysterious mountain on the outskirts of town
On the outskirts of Iino is the source of its UFO fame: Mt Senganmori.
Aso described it as a "mysterious mountain" where there have been "loads of UFO sightings".
Its triangular shape has given rise to local legends it is an ancient pyramid; other theories focus on its apparent strong magnetic field, or its strange rock formations.
It was near the top of Mt Senganmori where Toshie Aso saw the glowing light as a student.
Aso said back then it was a "bit embarrassing" to admit you had seen a UFO, but that had changed since she started working at the UFO Museum.
"I've been able to say 'I've seen one' with my head held high."
The museum was built near the base of the mountain a little more than 30 years ago and a UFO Research Institute was added in 2021.
'One or two' more would make a difference to Iino
In the centre of town, local fish ship owner Matsuzaki Kyoji has painted his face green and donned goggle-eye glasses for the UFO festival.
"Iino really is a lovely town," he said.
"I hope that the number of people who want to live here will increase — even if it's just by one or two people."
Iino's problems aren't unique: Japan's rapidly aging and shrinking population was recently described as a "national crisis".
In 2008, Iino was absorbed into the nearby Fukushima City, part of a nationwide program that almost halved the number of cities, towns and villages.
The mayor of Fukushima City, Baba Yuki, is full of praise for Iino's efforts during "challenging times".
"Iino Town has, after all, long been known as the 'UFO Village', so I hope we can all share this small resource together," he said.
"Indeed, as we have 'aliens' visiting us from all over the country today."
Matsuzaki sold out of food at his fish shop on festival day, but generally he hasn't seen a big boost in business from the UFO tourism.
"To be honest, this shopping street hasn't really been affected much," he said.
While people travel to see the UFO museum, they don't always come into the town centre.
But he remains hopeful — and US President Donald Trump could be the one to help.
How does Donald Trump come into it?
In February, Trump ordered federal agencies to identify and declassify documents relating to UFOs, UAPs and extraterrestrials.
Seven tranches of files have been released so far, with the latest batch of documents published last month.
The releases have included military footage, sworn statements from federal agents, radar data and historical records.
There are details of silent triangular-shaped craft with no visible propulsion, glowing orbs, strange light patterns and erratic or unexplained flight movements.
A US government office set up to investigate UAP named the region from western Japan to China as a "hotspot" for sightings.
In Iino, festival organisers and museum staff believed the Pentagon releases were increasing interest in the town.
The releases have also been considered by a Japanese parliamentary group, set up to investigate the national security implications of UAP.
Yoshiharu Asakawa helped establish the group when he was an MP and he now serves as an assistant to the group's chairman, a former defence minister.
"When such objects appear, the US gathers information, analyses it and attempts to determine what they are," he said.
"However, the Japanese Ministry of Defence and the government do not have such a system in place."
The parliamentary group has proposed a central agency be set up to scrutinise the documents being released by the US, and to respond to UAP sightings.
"The most immediate risk is whether the Self-Defence Forces can properly identify the latest drones from countries such as China, or reconnaissance balloons," Mr Asakawa explained.
"We are also considering what would happen if the latest weapons from another country were to appear in the airspace above a nuclear power station."
The group has pointed to a lack of coordination when three unidentified lights were seen over a nuclear power plant in the country last year.
Asakawa said the MPs weren't discussing aliens, and officials in the United States have also stressed there was no evidence of extraterrestrial life.
But that won't dull the enthusiasm in Iino.
Toshie Aso said meeting visitors to the UFO Museum had reaffirmed her own belief.
"I've been listening to all sorts of people's stories and thinking: 'Wow, that's incredible. So, it really is true. They do exist; they're out there.'
"That's the feeling I have every day."
